title: What deployment strategies do you use and how do they differ — rolling update, blue-green (two environments, instant switch + instant rollback), and canary (shift a % of traffic, observe, then ramp)?
shortTitle: Deployment Strategies — Rolling Update, Blue-Green, and Canary

s1_definition.profdef: A deployment strategy is how you replace a running version of a service with a new one while controlling risk and downtime. A rolling update replaces instances gradually, a few at a time, so there is always capacity serving traffic and no downtime, but during the roll both versions run together. Blue-green keeps two complete environments, blue (current) and green (new); you deploy and test green fully, then flip a load balancer or router to send all traffic to green instantly, and roll back instantly by flipping back. Canary releases the new version to a small percentage of traffic first, observes metrics such as error rate and latency, and only ramps to 100% if the canary is healthy, otherwise it aborts.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of upgrading the teller counters at a National Bank of India branch. A rolling update is closing one counter at a time, upgrading it, and reopening it before touching the next, so the branch never fully closes but for a while some counters are old and some are new. Blue-green is building a second identical branch next door, fully fitting it out and testing it while the old one serves customers, then overnight redirecting everyone to the new branch with one sign change, and if anything is wrong you just point the sign back. Canary is sending only a handful of customers to the new counter first and watching closely; if they are served well you send more and more, but if they complain you quietly pull that counter before most customers ever saw it.
s1_definition.oneliner: Rolling swaps instances gradually with no downtime, blue-green flips all traffic between two full environments for instant switch and rollback, and canary shifts a small percentage first and ramps only if metrics stay healthy.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A deployment strategy is how you replace a running version of a service with a new one while controlling risk and downtime. A rolling update replaces instances gradually, a few at a time, so there is always capacity serving traffic and no downtime, but during the roll both versions run together. Blue-green keeps two complete environments, blue (current) and green (new); you deploy and test green fully, then flip a load balancer or router to send all traffic to green instantly, and roll back instantly by flipping back. Canary releases the new version to a small percentage of traffic first, observes metrics such as error rate and latency, and only ramps to 100% if the canary is healthy, otherwise it aborts.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of upgrading the teller counters at a National Bank of India branch. A rolling update is closing one counter at a time, upgrading it, and reopening it before touching the next, so the branch never fully closes but for a while some counters are old and some are new. Blue-green is building a second identical branch next door, fully fitting it out and testing it while the old one serves customers, then overnight redirecting everyone to the new branch with one sign change, and if anything is wrong you just point the sign back. Canary is sending only a handful of customers to the new counter first and watching closely; if they are served well you send more and more, but if they complain you quietly pull that counter before most customers ever saw it.

**One line to remember:** Rolling swaps instances gradually with no downtime, blue-green flips all traffic between two full environments for instant switch and rollback, and canary shifts a small percentage first and ramps only if metrics stay healthy.

sections.s2_technical:
A rolling update is the Kubernetes default. The Deployment has a `strategy` of type `RollingUpdate` with `maxUnavailable` and `maxSurge` controlling how many pods can be down and how many extra can be created during the roll. Kubernetes brings up new-version pods, waits for them to pass their readiness probe, then terminates old-version pods, repeating until all pods run the new version. The upside is no downtime and simple configuration. The nuance is that both versions serve traffic simultaneously during the roll, so the new version must be backward compatible with the old, especially for database schema and message formats, and rollback means rolling back the other way which takes time.

Blue-green uses two full environments. Blue runs the current version and takes all production traffic; green is a parallel environment where you deploy the new version and run full smoke and acceptance tests against it with no customer traffic. When green is verified, you switch the router or Service selector so all traffic goes to green at once. The switch is near-instant, and rollback is equally instant because you just point back to blue, which is still running untouched. The cost is you need double the capacity during the cutover, and like rolling, any shared database must be compatible with both versions during the overlap.

Canary is the most gradual and metric-driven. You deploy the new version alongside the old but route only a small slice of traffic to it, for example 5%, using a service mesh like Istio or an ingress weight. You then watch key signals: error rate, latency percentiles, and business metrics such as failed transfers. If the canary stays healthy you ramp the weight to 25%, 50%, then 100%; if any signal degrades you set the weight back to 0% and abort, so only a small fraction of users were ever affected. Canary gives the earliest, lowest-blast-radius detection of a bad release, at the cost of more tooling and automation to measure and decide.

Choosing between them depends on risk and infrastructure. Rolling is the sensible default for stateless services where brief version overlap is fine. Blue-green suits releases where you want a clean, instant, all-or-nothing switch and can afford double capacity, which is attractive for a core banking service during a tightly controlled release window. Canary suits high-traffic, high-risk changes where you want real production signal before full exposure, such as a change to the fraud-scoring model.

A senior nuance that applies to all three is database compatibility. Because old and new versions coexist (during the roll, during the blue-green overlap, or during the canary), schema changes must be done in backward-compatible steps, often called expand-and-contract: first add the new column or table without removing the old, deploy code that writes both, then only after full rollout remove the old. Another nuance is that readiness and health probes are what make these strategies safe; without an accurate readiness probe, Kubernetes will send traffic to a pod that is not actually ready. A third nuance is automated rollback: a mature canary ties the traffic weight to an automated analysis (for example with Argo Rollouts or Flagger) so a bad release is rolled back without a human in the loop.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India used to take the transfer service fully offline to deploy, causing a visible maintenance window during which Rajesh and Priya could not move money. Customers complained. This is exactly the problem a rolling update solves. Instances are replaced a few at a time while the rest keep serving, so there is no downtime.

Problem 2 — A risky rewrite of the settlement engine needed a clean, instant cutover with the ability to abort immediately if the ledger numbers looked wrong, because a partial rollout of a ledger change is dangerous. This is exactly the problem blue-green solves. The new engine runs fully in green, is verified against real data copies, and traffic flips all at once, with an instant flip back to blue if anything is off.

Problem 3 — A change to the fraud-scoring rules could either catch more fraud or wrongly block thousands of legitimate transfers, and the team could not know which until real traffic hit it. This is exactly the problem canary solves. Five percent of traffic goes to the new rules first while the team watches the false-decline rate, ramping up only if it stays healthy and aborting instantly if it spikes.

To make this concrete without a real cluster we will write a Java simulation of a traffic router. We will model a `Router` that splits requests between an old version and a new version by weight, a `RollingUpdate` that gradually shifts instances, a `BlueGreen` that flips all traffic at once, and a `Canary` that ramps weight while checking a health signal and aborts on degradation. We will run all three against a stream of transfer requests so you can see how each handles the transition and how canary aborts a bad release. This mirrors the real strategies without needing Istio.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is an old version at a 1% error rate and several new versions deployed with different strategies.

Step 1: The rolling update starts with a router sending 0% to new. In steps of 25% it shifts traffic: 25% new, then 50%, then 75%, then 100%. At each step both versions are live and serving, which is why the new version must be backward compatible. The roll finishes with 100% on the new version and no downtime at any point.

Step 2: The blue-green switch deploys green version 2.0.0 and runs smoke tests. Because green's error rate of 2% is below the 10% smoke-test threshold, it passes. The router then flips from 0% to 100% new in a single step, an instant all-or-nothing cutover, while blue remains running so a rollback would be instant.

Step 3: The healthy canary begins at 5% traffic to new version 1.1.0 and observes a 2% error rate, which is under the 5% abort threshold, so it ramps to 25%, then 50%, then 100%, staying healthy at every step and finishing promoted to 100%.

Step 4: The bad canary begins at 5% traffic to the broken fraud rules, observes a 30% error rate, which exceeds the 5% threshold, so it immediately sets the weight back to 0% and aborts. Only the 5% slice ever saw the bad version, and no further ramp happened.

sections.s6_takeaway:
A deployment strategy is how I replace a running version with a new one while controlling risk and downtime, and I pick from three main approaches. A rolling update replaces instances gradually, a few at a time, so there is always capacity serving traffic and no downtime; its trade-off is that both versions run together during the roll, so the new version must be backward compatible. Blue-green keeps two complete environments, deploys and fully tests the new one with no customer traffic, then flips the router so all traffic moves at once; the switch and the rollback are both near-instant because the old environment stays running, at the cost of needing double capacity during the cutover. Canary releases the new version to a small slice of traffic first, watches error rate, latency, and business metrics, and only ramps to full if it stays healthy, aborting back to zero if anything degrades, which gives the smallest possible blast radius.

I choose based on risk and infrastructure. Rolling is my default for stateless services where brief version overlap is harmless. Blue-green suits a tightly controlled release of something like a settlement engine where I want a clean all-or-nothing switch and the ability to abort instantly. Canary suits high-risk, high-traffic changes such as a new fraud-scoring model, where I need real production signal before exposing everyone.

The one point I always stress because it applies to all three is database compatibility. Since old and new versions coexist during the roll, the blue-green overlap, or the canary, schema changes must be done in backward-compatible, expand-and-contract steps: add the new column first, deploy code that writes both old and new, and only remove the old column after the rollout is complete. I also rely on accurate readiness probes, because they are what stop Kubernetes from sending traffic to a pod that is not truly ready.

On the banking project I used rolling for most stateless services, blue-green for a risky settlement-engine rewrite so we could flip and, if the ledger numbers looked wrong, flip straight back, and canary with Argo Rollouts for a fraud-rules change where a bad release could wrongly block thousands of legitimate transfers. The senior point I always add is that the canary was wired to automated metric analysis, so if the false-decline rate spiked it rolled back to zero percent on its own without waiting for a human, which is exactly the safety you want when real customers' money is involved.
